rows.reasoning: Rationalizing choice ② gives 1/(sqrt(x+2)+2)→1/4, not 1/2. The other four limits evaluate to 8, 3, 0, and 2 respectively, so exactly choice ② is false.
Continuity requires 9−3m+3=0, so m=4. Then (x²−4x+3)/(x−3)=x−1 for x≠3, giving limiting value n=2. Hence m+n=6, choice ④.
For x≠2, f(x)=(sqrt(x−1)−1)/(x−2)=1/(sqrt(x−1)+1). Continuity gives f(2)=1/2, choice ①.
For x≠2, f(x)=(x+5). Differentiability at 2 requires continuity, so m+1=f(2)=7; therefore m=6, choice ③.
Continuity equates the one-sided limits: 1−2k=k−5, so k=2. Then f(0)=−3 and k+f(0)=−1, choice ②.
The derivative is 2x−1. Setting the tangent slope equal to 1 gives x=1 and y=5; the tangent is y−5=x−1, i.e. y=x+4, choice ④.
The secant slope on [1,2] is (−5−0)/(2−1)=−5. Since f'(x)=−4x+1, the equation f'(c)=−5 gives c=3/2, choice ③.

ㄱ is true by subtracting the two existing finite limits. ㄴ fails because existence of lim g(x) near a says nothing about continuity of g at lim f(x). ㄷ can fail when the denominator limit is zero, e.g. the resulting quotient diverges. ㄹ fails for f=sin(1/(x−a)), g=f−1, whose difference is constant. Only ㄱ is true: choice ①.
The increment from 1−3h to 1+h is 4h, so the quotient tends to 2f'(1). Thus f'(1)=3. Since f'(1)=3+2m−4=2m−1, m=2.
Differentiate f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)+6xy with respect to y and set y=0: f'(x)=f'(0)+6x=4+6x, choice ⑤.
f'(x)=3(x−1)², so the two tangency points of slope 3 occur at x=0,2. The tangents are y=3x+1 and y=3x−3. Their distance is 4/sqrt(3²+1²)=4/sqrt(10), choice ②.

From the opened graph, f(−2)>f(4), so the secant slope is negative. The curve has three descending branches between the interval endpoints; each contributes one tangent parallel to that secant, while the increasing branches contribute none. Thus there are 3 values of c, choice ③.

With the right shift g(x)=f(x−p), the second limit forces f(0)=f'(0)=0; the first finite positive limit then forces f(−p)=0. Since f is monic cubic, f(x)=x²(x+p). The first limit becomes 1/p and equals p, so p=1. Therefore g(2)=f(1)=2, choice ①.

On OA and OB the circle intersections appear for radii through 4 and 3; on AB the minimum radius is the altitude 12/5 and maximum is 4. The distinct-intersection count jumps at r=12/5, 3, and 4 (vertex coincidences included), so the sum is 12/5+3+4=47/5, choice ④.

C1 matching at x=−1 gives c=a−4 and d=b−2. For |f−p| to be differentiable, the two unbounded quadratic branches must touch level p at their vertices; equating vertex values yields a=2 and p=b−1, so f=p+(x+1)² on the left and f=p−(x+1)² on the right. The sole zero is at x=−1+sqrt(p), which must equal q because |f(x+q)| has its only cusp at x=0. From f(p)=p−(p+1)²=−21, p=4, q=1, and f'(q)=−4, choice ④.
By the derivative definition, f'(2)=12(2)²+1=49; directly expanding [f(2+h)−f(2)]/h also gives 49 in the limit.

The finite limit forces f(x)=x²+ax+b with integers a,b. The condition gives a=f(−4)=16−4a+b, hence b=5a−16. Since x/f(x) must be continuous for all real x, f has no real zero, so the discriminant (a−4)(a−16)<0 and integer a is 5 through 15. Then f(2)=7a−12 ranges from 23 to 93, whose sum is 116.

Since f(1)=−2 and f'(1)=−3, the tangent to y=(x²−3)f(x) at P is y=2x+2. The circle's center lies on the normal through P, C=(1,4)+t(2,−1), radius |t|sqrt(5). Tangency to x-axis requires radius 4−t; the first-quadrant solution is t=sqrt(5)−1, giving r=5−sqrt(5). Its area is π(5−sqrt(5))²=π(30−10sqrt(5)).
